name: Breath mints

image.caption: Tic Tac Breath Mints, at Costco, 6/2015, by Mike Mozart of TheToyChannel and JeepersMedia on YouTube #Tic #Tac #Breath #Mints

lead: Breath mints are mint-flavoured candies eaten to freshen breath before or after social occasions. They are cheap, portable and work within moments.

The strong mint flavour covers odour, and sugar-free types may also stimulate saliva. Dental sources and Wikipedia describe the effect as short-term masking rather than treatment of the cause of odour. Few clinical trials have tested mints specifically; one compared oxidising lozenges with mints and gum for malodour.

paras: People keep a tin handy and use one before meetings, dates or close conversations, often alongside brushing and rinsing for longer-lasting freshness.
Generally low risk; peppermint may worsen reflux, and some mints contain sweeteners that bother sensitive people.

angle.text: Breath mints give fresh-smelling breath quickly, before or after social occasions. Dental sources and Wikipedia describe the effect as short-term masking rather than treatment of the cause of odor.

lead: Breath mints are small mint-flavoured candies eaten to make breath smell fresher before or after social contact.[1] They are one of the quickest appearance-related tools available: a mint takes seconds to use, fits in a pocket, and changes how close conversation, dating and interviews feel to the person using it. Hard mints, soft mints and Scotch-style mints with a hard shell and softer centre are all sold, flavoured with peppermint, spearmint, wintergreen or non-mint flavours.[1]

Dental sources and Wikipedia's halitosis article describe mints and similar over-the-counter products as short-term masking: they cover odour for a period rather than removing its cause, which in most genuine cases is bacteria on the back of the tongue or gum disease.[2][2] Sugar-free versions may also stimulate saliva, and saliva is part of how the mouth keeps odour down.[3]

Published clinical work on mints themselves is small. One study compared oxidising lozenges with two brands of mints and chewing gum on judged odour, and another tested sorbitol-sweetened mints on salivary flow in people with dry mouth.[4][3] Mints also appear in dental trials as a comparison or placebo product.[5]
infobox: Altoids, Ice Breakers, Tic Tac, Polo[1]

paras: Hard mints are boiled-sugar style candies and include pinwheel mints, humbugs and the best-known tinned and pocket-pack brands such as Altoids, Ice Breakers and Tic Tac, which also come in non-mint flavours.[1] Soft mints, sold as butter or dinner mints, dissolve more readily and often contain more butter. Scotch mints, also called mint imperials or pan drops, are white, round candies with a hard shell and softer centre, popular in Britain, other Commonwealth countries and Europe.[1]

Flavour comes from mint or wintergreen oil, or from artificial flavourings; Wikipedia notes that many popular mints list little or no real peppermint or spearmint oil.[1] Sugar-free mints use polyols such as sorbitol or high-intensity sweeteners such as aspartame, which is among the additives approved by the US FDA for use in breath mints.[6]

Wikipedia dates mints as a distinct product to the 18th century, although it flags the sources for that early date as weak.[1] Their popularity rose in the early 20th century with urbanisation and mass advertising that stressed convenience and the social cost of bad breath, often aimed at young people.[1] Early packaging used cardboard boxes and tins, and later formats included paper or foil rolls, plastic boxes and individually wrapped mints.[1] In the United States a 2016 FDA final rule amended the label serving size for breath mints.[7]

Mints deliver a strong flavour and cooling sensation that overlays the odour in the mouth. Sugar-free mints can also raise salivary flow, which a 1989 study of people with dry mouth measured over a 10-minute test period.[3]

Halitosis is usually traced to bacteria on the tongue and gums producing volatile sulphur compounds, and Wikipedia estimates that most genuine cases originate in the mouth; additional causes include dry mouth, smoking, garlic and onion, tonsil stones, sinus problems and reflux.[2] Mints do not act on these sources, which is why sources describe them as short-term masking and why dental advice centres on brushing, tongue cleaning, flossing and treating gum disease.[2][2]

In a 1997 randomised study of 123 young adults, volunteers were assigned to one of six groups, including two brands of breath mints, sugar-free gum without actives, regular and full-strength oxidising lozenges, or no treatment. Judges rated whole-mouth and tongue odour, and volatile sulphide levels were measured 24 hours after baseline. Only the full-strength oxidising lozenge significantly reduced tongue-dorsum odour on the spoon test; the mints were not distinguished from control on that measure.[4]

A 1989 study found that a sorbitol-sweetened breath mint increased whole and parotid salivary flow in people with dry mouth over 10 minutes and reduced the drop in plaque pH after a sucrose rinse.[3] In a 4-week trial of 78 adults with gingivitis, breath mints served as the control while a baking-soda chewing gum was tested; the gum group had a 17 percent plaque reduction versus about 9 percent in the mint group.[5]

Most breath-odour trials in the literature test toothpastes and rinses; for example, trials of triclosan-copolymer toothpaste rated breath odour 12 hours after brushing.[8][9] Wikipedia notes that tentative evidence supports chlorhexidine or cetylpyridinium chloride rinses and tongue cleaning, and that evidence does not support a benefit from chewing gum for halitosis.[2]

Mints are generally an everyday food. Some contain aspartame, which must carry a phenylalanine warning for people with phenylketonuria, and a 1988 review discussed reports of intolerance reactions in some individuals.[6] Peppermint may relax the lower oesophageal sphincter and aggravate heartburn or reflux, according to Wikipedia.[1] Sugar-containing mints add sugar to teeth, one reason sugar-free types are common.[3]

Wikipedia also notes that a small share of people who believe they have bad breath have none that others can detect, and that persistent odour can be a sign of gum disease or another condition worth having examined.[2]

In appearance discussion mints are treated as a convenience item: a pocket tin handled before a date, interview or close conversation, used alongside brushing, flossing and tongue cleaning. Mentions on forums such as T Nation are mostly incidental, for example people using mints during cutting diets or before job interviews.[10]

lore.intro: Mints are discussed as a convenient, cheap breath fix to use alongside oral hygiene, and mostly mentioned in passing.[10]
